title: From Econometrics to Scenario Thinking
text:
For a long time, most of my research began with data from the past.
I worked with econometric models to examine relationships, test hypotheses and understand how economic, technological and environmental variables moved together. The questions were usually backward-looking in the best sense of the term: what happened, what was associated with what, and what can the observed data tell us?
That way of thinking is still important to me. But my PhD has gradually pushed me toward a different kind of question.
Instead of asking only what happened?, I now spend much more time asking:
What could happen? What would have to change for it to happen? Where would those changes fall? And what would implementation look like for different people and places?
That shift sounds small, but it changes the entire research process.
Econometrics usually begins with observed variation. Scenario thinking often begins with a future condition, a policy target or a set of assumptions that may never have existed in the historical data. A country may set a climate-neutrality target for 2050, for example. There is no historical dataset showing how that exact transition already happened. The researcher has to construct plausible pathways, make assumptions explicit and test what follows from them.
This is where scenario modelling, foresight and backcasting become useful.
Strategic foresight is not simply forecasting. The OECD describes it as a way of exploring multiple plausible futures and preparing for the opportunities and challenges they may create. The European Commission similarly emphasises that scenarios are not predictions. They are ways of thinking systematically about how different futures might unfold.
Backcasting turns the direction around again. Instead of projecting today’s trends forward, it starts with a future objective and asks what would have to happen between that future and the present.
I find that distinction especially useful for climate, agriculture and land-use policy. A target can be clear at national level while saying very little about implementation. If livestock numbers change, where does that adjustment occur? If land is released, what can it realistically support? If a policy looks affordable in aggregate, are its costs concentrated among particular farms or regions?
Those are not questions that one method can answer on its own.
I have also learned that the divide between econometrics and scenario modelling is not as clean as it first appears. Econometric models can support forecasts and counterfactual scenarios, and historical evidence can discipline assumptions about future behaviour. In energy policy, researchers have long combined top-down economic models with more detailed sector or technology models because each sees something the other misses.
So I do not think of my research as moving away from econometrics.
It feels more like moving from a single window to a room with several windows.
Econometrics helps me ask what the observed world can teach us. Scenario modelling asks what different future worlds might require. Spatial models ask where change would occur. Microsimulation asks how apparently uniform policies can produce very different effects across heterogeneous units.
The interesting part is not choosing one of them.
It is knowing which question each method is capable of answering, and where its limits begin.

Further reading

OECD Strategic Foresight
European Commission: How do we build scenarios in a foresight exercise?
UK Government Futures Toolkit

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
National AFOLU pathways can specify how livestock numbers, land release and future land uses change without showing where those changes fall.
GOBLIN-Spatial asks:

When a nationally coherent agricultural transition requires restructuring, where does transition pressure concentrate, what can the released land support, and can competing future land-use requirements be accommodated within the available geography?

GOBLIN supplies the national pathway. GOBLIN-Spatial resolves its geography and tests spatial feasibility.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
How it works
National GOBLIN pathway
        ↓
Transition incidence
Where does adjustment fall?
        ↓
Spatial response potential
What can released land support?
        ↓
Spatial transformability
Can competing future land uses fit?
        ↓
Spatial flexibility
Is one geography necessary?
The framework is a spatial stress-test of transition pathways, not a prediction of individual farmer or parcel decisions.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
Evidence and scale
The historical reconstruction covers 2015–2025 and is anchored to the 2020 Census of Agriculture at Electoral Division level. Higher-level livestock controls maintain national accounting consistency while preserving validated local structure.
The model combines agricultural statistics with land, soil and drainage information, LPIS context and explicit eligibility controls.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
What it does not claim
The model does not predict individual farmer behaviour, household welfare, market prices, parcel-level adoption or the exact geography that will exist in 2050.
Those questions require behavioural, farm-level or market models.

title: BioLand-US
text:
BioLand-US asks a practical implementation question:

When a techno-economic model allocates land to perennial biomass, how much of that prospective allocation can also be supported by compatible agricultural land and voluntary contractual participation?

The model does not replace or re-optimise the upstream resource allocation. It adds an explicit implementation layer.

title: BioLand-US
text:
Scientific logic
The framework keeps four quantities distinct:
Techno-economic biomass allocation
        ↓
Compatible agricultural land
        ↓
Contractually accessible land
        ↓
Prospectively mobilised biomass
This makes it possible to distinguish technical allocation from land compatibility and actual access through voluntary contracts.

title: IFT-BioSim
text:
IFT-BioSim asks how a common national transition objective can create very different economic pressures across heterogeneous farms.
It focuses on who bears adjustment, who responds, and how policy design changes incidence.

title: IFT-BioSim
IFT-BioSim
text:
Why it matters
A technically feasible national pathway does not reveal how costly the transition may be for particular farms. IFT-BioSim is designed to make that distribution visible and to test whether alternative compensation or incentive designs change the burden.

title: Forecasting asks what will happen. Foresight asks what could.
text:
FORESIGHT project illustration, FUSION, University of Galway, used under CC BY-SA 4.0.


A forecast asks what is likely to happen. Foresight asks something different: which futures are possible, what would it take to reach them, and what do we learn by working backwards from the outcome?
The distinction sounds academic. In agricultural climate policy, it is practical, and it shapes much of the work I now do.
I do my PhD within FUSION, a modelling group at the University of Galway that works across life-cycle assessment, integrated assessment, land-use analysis and environmental software. Much of my work connects to FORESIGHT, a project funded by Ireland’s Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications under a services contract to provide agriculture and land-use modelling to the Climate Action Modelling Group. The project is led by FUSION with the University of Limerick and FERS Ltd.
I mention the funding at the start because I will write about Irish climate and agricultural policy on this site, and readers should know where I sit. The views expressed here are my own.
Within FORESIGHT, GOBLIN is used as a national land-balance modelling framework for exploring agriculture, forestry and other land-use pathways through backcasting. Rather than predicting what Ireland will do, the approach can begin with a future objective such as climate neutrality and examine combinations of livestock, forestry, wetlands and cropland that could be consistent with it.
That is foresight in practice.
My own question begins where a nationally coherent pathway can become much less simple.
A national reduction in cattle numbers, for example, could fall very differently across a dairy-intensive area and a region dominated by suckler farming. The aggregate change may be identical while the consequences for production systems, land use and local economies are not. That is an illustration of the question, not a result.
I am interested in resolving national pathways down to places and farms: where adjustment falls, what released land can realistically support, and how economic and behavioural differences change the picture.
What I value most about working this way is a lesson I keep relearning: the model is not the product.
The useful product is better evidence for a difficult decision, produced transparently enough that assumptions can be examined and alternatives tested.
Future posts here will range much more widely than my PhD. I will write about climate and agricultural policy, land use, energy, economics, Ghana and Ireland, useful models and code, books, technology and research life.
The aim is simple: to think in public, and to make technical arguments readable without flattening them.

title: About
text:
I am Elvis Kwame Ofori, a Ghanaian researcher and writer based in Ireland.
My path has taken me from Ghana to China and now Ireland, and that movement between places has shaped the way I think about policy. I am interested in how national decisions look very different once they reach households, farms, firms and communities.

Research
I am a PhD Researcher and Research Assistant in Plant & AgriBiosciences at the University of Galway’s Ryan Institute. My doctoral work focuses on how agricultural, climate and land-use transitions distribute costs, opportunities and constraints across farms and places.
I work within the wider FUSION and FORESIGHT modelling environment at the University of Galway. My doctoral research is supervised by David Styles and Cathal O’Donoghue.
